stem: Why is asymptomatic bacteriuria generally not treated in children?

options.text: The bacteria are usually not viable and will not grow in culture
It is expensive and requires intravenous antibiotics
Treatment can increase antibiotic resistance and replace normal flora with more virulent organisms
It is always caused by Staphylococcus, which does not respond to antibiotics
It always progresses to symptomatic urinary tract infection if untreated

explanation: Treatment can increase antibiotic resistance and disrupt normal flora, allowing more virulent organisms to replace harmless bacteria.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect because bacteriuria means bacteria are present, even when the child has no symptoms.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because the main reason to avoid treatment is not cost or route of administration, but antimicrobial stewardship and microbiome effects.
optionExplanations.C: Correct because unnecessary antibiotics can select resistant organisms and disturb the normal flora, which may allow more virulent bacteria to overgrow.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because asymptomatic bacteriuria is not always caused by Staphylococcus, and organism type does not change the general rule against treatment in an asymptomatic child.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because asymptomatic bacteriuria does not always progress to symptomatic infection, so routine treatment is not recommended solely to prevent this.

source.hint: Consider the long-term ecological consequences of using antibiotics when no clinical illness is present.
